topic: Cleveland Court - - Submitted 4/1/2020 at 3:28 p.m.
comment: Esteemed Council Members, I am writing you about some concerns that I have of holding Council meetings in a business as normal fashion. Things are not normal I have several issues. I received my notice for the meeting last week and since then have spoken with 4 of my close neighbors and 3 of the 4 were not aware of it. They or their spouses have not seen or received notices. I know that all 3 (6) of them are opposed to the changes. Fortunately I informed them of the meeting so they can participate. Under normal circumstances I would copy my notice knock on doors and encourage my neighbors to participate in the process. I am very reluctant to do that under current conditions and it would be socially unacceptable for me to do so. I have always attended public meetings in person, I have face timed a few times and it is a poor substitute for being there. I prefer to hear everything see people's faces and reactions etc. Also I am technologically challenged and don't own a computer so it my be difficult or impossible for myself and others to participate in the meetings. I feel it is unfair to the residents of our neighborhood to limit our ability to meaningfully engage in the public process. When we can't personally interact with each other it severely diminishes our ability to organize and voice our collective concerns. At the Planning Commission meeting there was a large number of people in attendance some of which made comments some that didn't. There were 14 comments against 1 for ,an associate of the developers, and the changes still passed overwhelmingly. The petitioners seem to always have the advantage,all they have to do is sit back and wait for the normal outcome. I would hope that in the current conditions it would be considered to postpone all meetings 60-90 days or at the least extend the comment period and decision for 60-90 days so that all those concerned can have their voices herd as we try to protect our surroundings. We all have much more immediate and pressing things to do! Please help us by doing what we should all be doing, putting off business as normal for a month or two. Thank You, Eric Miller

subject: Cleveland Court - - Submitted
topic: Cleveland Court - - Submitted 4/3/2020 at 1:58 p.m.
comment: Esteemed City Council Members. I hope you are doing well dispite our current situation. I am writing you about zoning changes for a proposed development, Hearthstone II. Within the last 30 years I have lived ■■■■■■■ for 30 years or more, so I had time things have changed a bit, mostly for the better. Originally the parcel in question had a small two story house with a garage and a shed or two. An elderly couple lived there.I rarely ever saw them. At some point the husband passed away and it was just the wife for 15 years or so. She didn't drive but her children would visit now and again. After she died the house was vacant. It was purchased by two contractors that I am acquainted with, one of them owned the house directly to the north. They obtained a zoning change so that they could put 3 units on the lot instead of the maximum of 2 it was originally zoned for. I attended that meeting and all there except those 2 were opposed to those changes. Of course they received their change. That development never happened for several reasons and the lot has been unused for a number of years. At some point someone purchased the lot in question and the house and lot to the north. Both parcels were then re-subdivided, shrinking the lot to the north and enlarging the one to the south. Now there was enough room to put 5 units on the southern parcel. The current developers want to have the zoning changed to accommodate 7 units. From a large lot with a small house, fruit tree, grass, a cooling summer breeze, and a Little Old Lady how didn't own a car lived, to a 7 unit complex that fills the lot to the edges, 7 groups of tenants with all their cars, trailers motorcycles and stuff. That is basically a 700% increase in usage over what it has been for the last 30 years! Myself and many of my neighbors attended the Planning Commission meeting in January, over their request to make that part of the 15 comments 14 were in opposition to the changes, the only one for, was obviously from an associate of the developers. We have many concerns; parking, congestion,set backs, noise, view, etc. but the number of units was shared by virtually everyone as the major concern. Most of the apartments in the vicinity are 4 units a couple are 5. most of us realize that we can't stop development but agree, reluctantly, that 5 units might be acceptable but 7 is too many! The Planning Commission after listening to our opinions made a few comments to us. One member told us she had done her "due diligence" and driven by the parcel a couple of times, a Sunday morning and a weekday evening, she didn't get out of her car! She thought there was plenty of on street parking in the area and that most of our concerns were negligible, and stated, we were just " afraid of change." Several of us taking together afterword thought her attitude was dismissive and condescending. We were all surprised and disappointed when they voted almost unanimously in favor of the zoning changes. It seems our opinions don't matter and had little or no influence at all, even though we are the ones that live there. My wife and I own a well maintained home directly east of the proposed development. Originally on of the developers bought my current home I lived near Sugar House Park and used it frequently. There was a Public hearing for the first office building to be built to the west of the park. Many of the people at the meeting were concerned that the multi story building would block the sunset view that we enjoyed from the park. The developers and zoning commission assured everyone that the building and future development would not block the view. You can still see, or not, the results. That office building is still 3 stories or more above street level and subsequent developments have blocked most of the rest of the horizon. It seems that these types of results are the norm from this and other situations I've seen and been involved with over the years. It seems that this is what we get when we trust the Authorities and developers to do what the majority desire. It seems that the only real concerns are how they can maximize tax revenue, and profits for the developers. It does not seem to matter what the residents want, and we are the ones that live with the results. I have several concerns with this development that will impact all of the local residents. The first and I think the largest is the lack of off street parking and the congestion that will be created. There is a 4 unit apartment 2 lots south of me that has 12 vehicles associated with it, I have the pictures. The new development in question has 7 units with 8 parking slots, at the minimum I would expect at least 14 vehicles to be parked in the vicinity and that number could easily be higher. There could easily be 6-10 or more cars parked on the street. This could create several problems,especially considering the narrowness of Cleveland Ave. which already has very limited space, with a small number of parking spaces on one side only. Several of these spaces are already frequently used by current residents. Emergency vehicles may be hindered! There will not be anywhere for visitors to park, and it will much more difficult for all traffic to navigate a street that can already be tough at times.There are also potential problems when it comes to snow removal. It will be difficult with all the parked cars, narrow set backs, lack of parking strips, driveways and sidewalks, there is very little space to pile snow. With the proposed set backs the buildings will only be about 5' from the sidewalk and about 9' from the street, there is no parking strip on either side and the homes on the south side of Cleveland are close to the street as well. There are several other concerns such as noise, privacy, parking in my driveway and other people's driveways, but the biggest one is the alley. From the alley to the east entrance and exiting the alley will be difficult. I already have to jockey my way in at times because of parked cars when I am in my work truck, this will likely be a daily occurrence when this development is completed, regardless of the number of units. When exiting it will be difficult for us to see cross traffic from the east as the building will block the view and the view to the west is already almost completely blocked by a fence, a result of poor zoning regulations. It is inconvenient at least and potentially dangerous for those of us that use the alley. The residents on the west side of the development will likely find it difficult to access their garages because of the set backs. One of them is about 16' from the edge of the alley, mine is over 22' and I can just barely make it in and out without jockeying around, and I have a tight turning radius. Access for the garbage and recycling bins could also be difficult at Cleveland Court, and for the garbage truck that services the apartments along the alley. Also, with narrow set backs and 30' tall walls there will be a micro climate that could drastically affect the current residents to the south and also those move in to the complex. It will be like living in an oven and with the layout of the complex there will be little chance of cooling breezes. Andrew, Hiedi and their children who live to the north will no longer enjoy sunshine coming through their windows, maybe a little at the height of summer. Instead they will be enjoying the growl of 7 AC compressors day and night all summer long, and a blank slab of wall 30' tall instead of a view of the mountains. Several of the neighbors to the west are also concerned about their blocked view. In addition these tall walls on all 4 sides are mostly slabs with garage doors and few windows, it would be more appropriate in an industrial complex than in a neighborhood with about 95% single family homes that are more traditional architecturally. There is very little engagement with the the community and unless the design has changed all access is from the internal courtyard. No sitting on the porch and saying hello to the neighbors. It is similar to designs I have seen in the Middle East and other areas where they have tall walls, no windows, a fortified entrance and a"Courtyard." One of the goals with the zoning changes is to engage the neighborhood and fit in. This development will do neither. These zoning changes make no sense, other than dollars. We are not close to any major transit lines Trax etc. only a normal bus route on 5th east. An acquaintance of mine that used transit regularly found it slow and difficult to use in this area. An extra 2 units will have little affect on the housing marketing in this area, but it will negatively affect our neighborhood and likely be less desirable for those who might choose to move in to Cleveland Court. Even if the existing zoning is left in place, 5 units instead of 7, increased set backs on the front and sides and an increased set back on the north, all of these concerns and many more will still exist. It will still degrade the quality of life in the neighborhood in these and many other ways, just a little less. It would be nice if we could think a little more about Quality of life, not Quantity of life. Please Council Members, for the benefit of all of the residents in the area, myself, and the future residents of Cleveland Court, I hope you can take some time to come and visit our neighborhood in the next few days, if you haven't already. Please get out of your car and walk around for a little while, experience the surroundings first hand, and think about the unique circumstances involved in this zoning decision. Use your insight to envision what it could be like in the future. And please encourage the other council members to do likewise, We would greatly appreciate it! You and your fellow council members are our last hope to preserve the character of "Our" neighborhood. We would prefer a Community Garden a micro park or single family home, 4 units instead of 5 would be nice. Seven units is Unacceptable! We are not afraid of change, just change that will diminish our quality of life! Thank you for your time, and your service to our community. Sincerely, Eric Miller

subject: Cleveland Court Rezone & Master Plan Amendment
topic: Cleveland Court Rezone & Master Plan Amendment
comment: Dear Council members, I would like to express my support for this proposal. I live about a block away. This development is located within a cluster of higher density zoning in the middle of Liberty Wells. Several other higher density developments have also been built in the close proximity. I think this is totally appropriate. One of the issues facing SLC is the lack of affordable housing. Fundamentally it is an economic issue of supply and demand. There is a significant demand and mush less supply - hence higher prices. How are we ever going to provide the supply if we don't build housing!!! Most everyone agrees that we should have more housing - - but they think it should be built somewhere else. Unfortunately this is the same complaint you here everywhere so if one gave excessive weight to this issue, very little housing would ever be built. Another argument in reference to this particular development and the reason for the rezone is to allow a couple of more units so all of them will be a bit more affordable. Complaints I have heard at the Liberty Wells Community Council is not surprisingly - parking. Or the implication that there isn't enough provided and there is a vast shortage of public parking in the surrounding area. As I recall all of the units have off street parking and there is plenty of on street parking for residents that have guests or a second car. To repeat - there is plenty of public parking in the adjacent neighborhood. Other complaints I have heard is that LW's is a single family neighborhood and a multi-unit development will somehow sully the neighborhood. To digress, I've never understood why some people think single family housing is sacrosanct as if it is a superior form of living. I don't agree. I think it is one of many choices that are available to all of us. To get to the point, LW's (I've lived here for almost 20 years) is not an exclusive single family home neighborhood. It is a nice mix of single family homes, some higher density housing, some small commercial businesses primarily in the interior, larger commercial on the perimeter and finally a very large park. In other words this is a real neighborhood! In conclusion, I feel that this project will benefit and fit in with the neighborhood and would encourage you to approve the rezone. Bill Davis

topic: Cleveland Court Rezone & Master Plan Amendment
comment: Dear members of the Council, I don't have the new system figured out yet. I am writing to express my opposition to the proposal before you tonight in the RMF-35 zone called Cleveland Court. 1 The applicant is ALWAYS distinct from the project. In this case, the applicant Peter Corroon is just fine, but the proposal is an example of the dysfunctional cherry picking that has been going on with respect to the zoning ordinance for years during the building frenzy. 2 There are plenty of places for increased density in the City at this point without sabotaging our lower density neighborhoods. The City has failed miserably to provide incentives for the redevelopment of nonconforming uses, surface parking lots, and single story commercial buildings. 3 The FBUN-1 and -2 were developed at the request of the RDA specifically for the West Gateway and were applied in a comprehensive rezoning there. The zones were adopted City wide unfortunately and have been applied piecemeal elsewhere. Some of you will recall that you had to fix the FBUN-2 because there were no setbacks unless the abutting zone was FBUN-1. In other words, these zones as developed were intended to be used as part of a comprehensive rezoning. 4 As someone who has lived in the Bryant neighborhood for 45 years, I will tell you that you do a profound disservice to a neighborhood when you give a property owner development rights which the abutting property owners do not have. That is the reality I live with; I can't do what my neighbors can do with their property. 5 Finally, I don't know how the City can think that it has a handle on compatibility when the proposal includes side-by-side garage doors as close as possible to the public sidewalk. I realize that the historic house has already been demolished and that there is a history of prior approvals and positive recommendations, but this cherry picking of zones needs to stop. We need to deal with our wonderful neighborhoods comprehensively, not erode them piecemeal. Sincerely, Cindy Cromer

topic: Cleveland Court Rezone & Master Plan Amendment
comment: This proposal misuses the FB-UN1 zone and should be rejected. Parking is important in the single family home neighborhood. In addition the front and rear and garage setbacks create what I call a modern brutalist architecture that is not appropriate in ann area that is trying to protect the many single family home zoning in the area. This rezone WILL encourage destruction of the blocks of single family home zoning across the street. Similar higher density housing in the area has become run down and attracts a lot of criminal activity and has caused a reputation of criminal activity. The area already has problem controlling crime in the area and increasing density would exacerbate the situation. Ironically, State Street is a few blocks away and could, should and would provide better mixed use and mixed income housing and that should be the priority. This project WILL replace a single family home. Single family home neighborhoods should be protected and walkable neighborhoods with mixed use and mixed income should be encouraged on streets like State Street. Look at the pictures in the Staff Report. They show single family homes surrounding the project. Multi family units within 3 blocks is not a good reason to destroy a single family home neighborhood. Note that a majority of a significant number of neighbors that attended the Planning Commission were furious at the proposal (many more than 2). Good government should not be making citizens angry. And I still love Peter Corroon.

topic: Cleveland Court Rezone & Master Plan Amendment
comment: Council, I would like to comment on the zoning changes for Cleveland Court. I am not opposed to something being built on the lot but I think the current zoning and setback allows for the developer to design and build an appropriate building. The proposed zoning change will set a precedence for future developers wanting to change from RMF-35 to FB-UN1. This change allow too much freedom for the contractor to do what they want. Lets keep FB-UN1 in the areas its supposed to be - near the transit lines. The smaller setbacks are going to be a safety issue. The driveway coming on the south side is only 10' -6", this doesn't allow a midsize car to even park temporary. Cars will parked over the sidewalk, creating people to walk in the road. this will only add to the traffic issue on Cleveland. Cleveland is already a skinny street having to back out is going to be tricky, then add in parked cars on the south most side. Cleveland is a thru street from 3rd to 4th east and no one goes 25 mph on it. Plus you add the parking on the south side and it becomes a one lane road. This becomes a real dangerous sidewalk for kids and parents to travel. A 5'-6" front yard is not an allowable amount of front yard. All the houses on Cleveland have at least 9'-6" of front or side yard. The goal of these developments are to create space that blends into existing neighborhood. By turning all the front yards into the center, this not only alienates the new residents but also the current ones from entering. This type of courtyard doesn't engage the neighborhood but pushes it away, to create its only micro neighborhood. I see this courtyard attracting homeless and criminals. I think the current zoning and setbacks should stand and not allow these changes. Thanks Josh Newton

topic: Cleveland Court Rezone & Master Plan Amendment
comment: SLC Council / Planners, I spoke in this evenings meeting regarding the Cleveland Court development on 1430 S 400 E - Parcel #16-18-204-032 (excuse my atypical nervousness). My comments felt a bit scattered and short, so I wanted to provide additional feedback via e-mail in a more organized fashion. As mentioned in the meeting, I am a licensed architect used to being on the other side of the microphone proposing projects and asking for zoning amendments, so I understand the process and am not anti-development. I do want the council to recognize their power to control RESPONSIBLE re-zoning and neighborhood in-fill development. The residents of this neighborhood would very much like to see this property developed with a size & unit appropriate project. This site is already zoned for a multi-family project (RMF-35)* zoning which should be more than adequate for an apartment / condo development to be designed and responsibly / sustainably executed. A few of my bulleted comments / concerns: - Zoning Change AND Planned Unit special exception ??? This project is seeking a Master Plan Amendment, Zoning Map Amendment, AND Planned Development modification. In short, they are asking to change the zoning, and in the same breath asking for an exception to the zoning regulation they are applying for. The developer representative mentioned the setbacks they are asking for are larger than code requires, but the diagram at the bottom of this e-mail (From the staff report) corrects that statement. Pandora's Box* This re-zoning precedent sets a dangerous example for irresponsible future development in our city. Allowing a property with no justifiable challenges to re-zone to form-based zoning for more units / density will open the flood gates to any parcel of land to justify zoning-free design moving forward. Form based zoning makes a lot of sense where it belongs in higher density, transit oriented development, NOT adjacent to a single bus-line in a residential neighborhood. Meet in the middle- As mentioned, would very much like to see this property developed, and not opposed to a multi-family project here, just want to make sure all factors are accounted for. I would ask that if the project is approved, they are required to adhere to current zoning regulations, setbacks, density, etc. * WIN-WIN! - Community Council Approval* . The developer representative mentioned the project was WIDELY approved in the Liberty Wells Community Council. I would like it to be on public record that NO pointed notices of this development were distributed to the surrounding neighbors regarding this particular topic. Although we did receive notices for both Planning Commission and City Council, we were unaware the process had begun months prior. Had we been able to voice our concerns earlier, the project design may have taken on a more acceptable shape to neighbors. Public Notice Distribution Requirements *I would ask that the council look at public notice distribution requirements to adjacent property owners and confirm at what point in the project they are required or not. If they are not required during community council phase, they should be as these are the most important voices in the process. Please let me know if these are required or not for community council meetings. Planning Commission Notes* Look back at previous meeting notes and you'll notice that the project was spoken against by +95% of attendees. The only positive comments were by developer representatives, NOT the residents of this neighborhood. Green Washing; Solar panels on the roof do not mean a project is sustainable* more interested in hearing about all electric options to HVAC systems design, alternative landscaping approaches, increased building envelope design, etc. Not enough information has been presented to date to make a case for this. Sustainable Requirements *I would ask that if the project is approved, that sustainable guidelines are mandated on the developer - i.e. LEED Residential, NGBS - National Green Building Standards, Energy Star, Utah High Performance Building Standards, or similar. If the city / community grants exceptions to the higher project density, unit count, and setbacks in the name of smaller, more sustainable units, the project should be truly held to more justifiable sustainability requirements. Parking / Traffic The residents of this area prefer the quieter walkable streets of this micro-hood to the busier neighboring thoroughfares of 500 E, 700 E, or 1300 S. We live on Blair Street, Cleveland, and 400 East because they are lower traffic, lower speed streets for our families. The proposed parking reduction requests will create additional vehicle traffic, parking challenges, vehicle congestion, and frustrated neighbors. Traffic / Parking Study Requirements* If this project is approved as proposed, I would ask that a full traffic and parking study analysis of the neighborhood is included in the final approvals factoring in realistic models of future vehicle use directly impacted by this development. As mentioned in this evenings meeting, Cleveland is already narrow, and deserves a decent set-back for the safety of the residents. Decreasing setbacks AND waiving parking requirements will create a safety issue for our neighborhood kids. In closing, would like to say thanks to SLC and the Council for keeping a positive attitude during these tough times. Thanks for organizing the online format for the City Council meeting so our voices can be heard. WebEx format is certainly not fool proof just yet, but definitely a positive start. Look forward to meeting my great new neighbors when the project is realized, and hope the council recognizes the responsible decision of approving an appropriately scaled unit count on this site. Funny that a few years ago when I was building a garage that uses the same alley as Cleveland Court, I was told I had to shrink my proposed 22x22 footprint to account for the square footage of my chicken coop in order to maintain 40% lot coverage. Long story short I tore down the chicken coop to accommodate the zoning / density requirements of SLC. I would ask the council look at the standing zoning for the site and require the developer to design within current city standards. Sorry for the long e-mail. Stay healthy and positive! Thanks, Ryan McMullen, AIA, LEED Green Associate Also, if the council has not already read the article below regarding the potential impact of this re-zone, I recommend they read the link below. https://www.buildingutahaia.com/form-based-zoning-coming-to-more-slc-neighborhoods-the-case-of-cleveland-court-in-liberty-wells/

topic: COVID-19
comment: To whom it may concern: I have learned that there are Salt Lake City Public Library services still operating during this pandemic. I am not a health expert, but I am concerned that continuing operation of any public library services poses a risk to Salt Lake City citizens considering the very public nature of all library work. This includes receiving and handling library materials. Also, the inter-library loan service of the public library seems particularly risky and could be a probable vector of the interstate spread of coronavirus. I am asking the mayor and city council to strongly consider ceasing all library operations and requiring all library staff to remain home until this public health crisis has abated. Thank you, Dominic Furano

topic: COVID-19
comment: Hello council members, I am writing to express my concern as to why Salt Lake County has not been issued a shelter-in-place order. I believe Summit County set a good example today by issuing a similar order and Salt Lake should follow that example. By the end of this week, 500,000 people around the world will have COVID-19, the US is on-track to pass Italy in the number of confirmed cases, and more than 20,000 people have died. As an EMT, a Master of Public Health student, and as someone who lives with two elderly people, one with pre-existing respiratory conditions, I am doing my part and staying home. But I have deep concerns that others are not taking this situation as seriously, as seen with the hundreds who gathered at the airport to greet returning missionaries. While Utah is not seeing the same number of cases as New York or Washington, without further stricter guidelines, I believe we will be there. Please help me protect my elderly parents and my patients by implementing a shelter in place order for Salt Lake City. Thank you, Emily Hacker

topic: COVID-19
comment: We risk losing many businesses that contribute to Salt Lake's diversity and embody its character; removing the buying power of individuals who own or work for local small businesses; incurring municipal, county, or state debt to bail out businesses, which will have to be paid back through increased taxes; and increasing the homelessness problem if people lose their jobs and have no other recourse. Again, Salt Lake can lead by example by keeping the local economy as strong as possible during this time. Finally, a shelter-in-place order or lockdown is impossible to enforce without imposing martial law. This would divert our police force from more pressing issues, such as the increase in domestic violence calls departments have recently received that are due, at least in part, to more people sharing close quarters in a stressful situation. Even if police were solely charged with keeping people in their homes, it would still be an impossible task. They cannot be everywhere at once, and it would require people to tell on their neighbors, which many wouldn't do. Most important, enforcing a shelter-in-place or lockdown is unconstitutional. Desperate times call for desperate measures, as the saying goes, but our current times are no more desperate than previous eras and we do still live in the United States after all. I want to close by emphasizing that I understand the complexity of this situation. Coronavirus poses many unknowns and I think everyone wants to help the most vulnerable members of our community. However, it is crucial we do not act out of fear and remain as rational as possible. For example, instead of bailing businesses out, can the state or county provide incentives to businesses to provide goods or services for combating the virus in some way? Such a measure would keep more people employed, give local businesses a boost, keep money flowing in our economy, and help mitigate coronavirus. Involving more people would also better educate the public, and get more individuals on board with current measures and guidelines. Thank you for all you have done so far. I am confident you are doing your best to handle this situation appropriately. Sincerely, Lucie Hacker

topic: COVID-19
comment: Dear Council Members, I wanted to write and say that I fully support an evictions freeze for people who cannot afford rent due to loss of work or hours because of coronavirus. But PLEASE, PLEASE do not give nuisance/criminal tenants a free pass while trying to protect those with genuine economic hardships in these troubling times. My husband and I have had to share a duplex with other tenants who have brought criminal activity to the property where our son lives, and we are terrified they will be even worse if they think there will be no consequences for their actions. Please do NOT give criminals, nuisances, and genuine lease-breakers a pass. Protect those with genuine hardship, but please, please DO NOT protect people who are just criminals from being deservedly evicted from a property where they are endangering a child's safety. Our landlord was preparing to move forward with getting them out and now we are terrified they will get to stay indefinitely and continue making us fear for our son's safety. The foot traffic thanks to the other tenants in our duplex is out of control, and at this point we have concerns about our health on top of the illegal activity. Please do NOT let them have a free pass or to benefit from protections meant for those facing genuine hardships rather than consequences for willful criminal and nuisance behavior. Thank you, Margaret C. SLC Citizen

topic: COVID-19

topic: Ellie Development and Preliminary Plat
comment: Greetings City Council Member, If the rezoning to Multi-Family residential contributes to the ELLIE DEVELOPMENT we would like you to VOTE AGAINST the rezoning change. We don't have an alternative plan, but we know that this project will displace the tenants that live next door in the Section 8 housing. The developer plans are to take down one of the section of the Country Oaks Apartments that is closest the property. If the families have to return to the shelter, they are at a higher risk of being exposed to the Covid-19 virus. Please consider this when you vote. We as a city have the capacity to stop gentrification and to create communities that holds people over profit. We are writing this letter to oppose the proposed Ellie Development and Preliminary Plat plan at 347, 353 & 359 North 700 West. Our neighborhood is being gentrified and working-class and poor families are being pushed out of the community. This new development would create an influx of more affluent residents and businesses. Creating upward rent pressure that will lead to the displacement of Rose Park residents. We cannot continue to repair neighborhoods at the cost of residents who have devoted their lives to creating these spaces. We cannot continue to increase attraction to an area by people with higher incomes spilling over from neighboring cities, towns, or states. We need more affordable housing complexes and not fancy, expensive apartments and condos. If this project is built, the first to be affected would be the Country Oaks Apartments I and II, a Section 8 housing complex that is home to more than thirty families. To preserve the integrity, character, and culture of Rose Park, please reconsider the development of this project and please consider this when you vote. Sincerely, Rose Park Brown Berets

comment: Hi there Ms. Mayor. I am a nurse with 30 years of experience. I am a Salt Lake City resident, and I urge you to reconsider your CDBG funding decision for The INN Between. Please keep The INN Between funded. I was the nursing supervisor for approximately 6 months during the time The INN Between went from their provisional to full state assisted living (AL) licensing. Prior to that, I was a case manager for 9 years at the Huntsman Cancer Hospital and the University of Utah Hospital. It was such a struggle to find placement for homeless patients who needed to be off the streets due to their medical condition. The U of U would write up contracts to "house" these patients in a skilled nursing facility where they really needed an AL which is less expensive for the taxpayers. Not to mention, how do we find a bed for a dying homeless patient?I have seen systems fail without investment in the disenfranchised population but I have also seen the beauty of it working really well. The VOA ACT team is one such example of money well spent. I think the city is best served by having a streamlined process with The INN Between, quality oversight and their funding continued. I hope your board and city council speak with professionals who deal with these issues on a day to day basis. Having had two son's who were homeless on the streets from serious mental illness I know the issues first hand, let alone professionally. Sincerely, Heidi Franke RN BSN University of Utah graduate of Nursing

comment: Dear Council Members, I am the Executive Director of Utah Health and Human Rights. We have provide wrap-around services for refugee, immigrant, and asylee survivors of torture for 17 years. I recognize that all the recommended CDBG projects focus on homeless services. I attended all the consolidated plan stakeholder meetings and am disheartened to see that programs that work tirelessly to prevent homelessness have been overlooked such as ours. 99% of our clients have income less than 50% of the MFI. Our clients have overcome the unimaginable in their home countries and continue to face obstacles with mental health, poverty, language and cultural barriers, physical health, and ongoing trauma. We are the only refugee service provider in Utah who provides services without time limits. Survivors can access our services no matter how long that have been in the U.S. and they can actively receive services for as long as they need, whether that is 8 months, or 8 years. Without our services many of our clients would face homelessness, generational poverty and trauma, and chronic physical health needs. I hope that you will consider funding our program as an essential service keeping Salt Lake City families from entering homelessness. Thank you, Heidi Justice Heidi Justice Executive Director Utah Health and Human Rights

comment: Hello Council: I am a Salt Lake City resident, and I urge you to reconsider your CDBG funding decision for The INN Between. Any amount that you can fund will help the sustainability of their program. As a former volunteer and public relations coordinator for the INN Between, I witnessed the achievement of this small group of people firsthand. I count as friends the residents who passed through those doors. Their colorful and tragic way of living left an indelible imprint that remains as part of the very fiber of my being. The thought of a funding loss for such a worthy program is painfully disheartening and for want of a better word, ludicrous. Given the COVID outbreak, so many homeless are helplessly forced into death even earlier. Denied services by hospitals all across the united states, they face horrendous conditions without help. The INN Between is one of only TWO such facilities in the entire United States able to provide services to those who are terminally ill and homeless. In and of itself, this is shameful. I am at a loss trying to fathom why you would cut funding. Kim Correa and her incredible staff are tirelessly devoted to ensuring quality care for each and every patient in this facility. For so many of us navigating the waters of COVID and staying alive is actually an ever-present goal. Up to three months ago, it wasn't even a thought. For the residents of the INN Between and all the homeless struggling to stay alive, this is the ever-present reality of daily living. Why would you want to participate in any effort to undermine this herculean effort and support for the downtrodden? Thank you for funding the INN Between, please keep doing so. Save lives instead of taking them away. Truly, Janet Jackson

comment: I am pleading to have continued funding for The Inn Between in this upcoming year; I speak as a family member of Patricia Rice who died there Nov. 7, 2019. She was diagnosed with cirrhosis from Hepatitis C in 2007, continued to work at a SLC company until her disability prevented her from doing acceptable work, @ 2013 when she went to full time disability through her employer and applied for Medicaid. She received a waiver through Salt Lake County Aging Services and was able to live pretty independently that way at Wasatch Manor with HUD funds until Sept. 2019 when too many falls made it impossible for her to live alone. Her hospice agency and SLCounty Aging services expedited her move to The Inn Between the first week of Sept 2019 and she was able to live there with some level of dignity and safety until her death. She was care for very tenderly and I have the greatest respect for all the staff and volunteers whose efforts let her die in dignity and peace. The population of poor and ill are the most voiceless in our community and I know we must speak for them when their care and protection are threatened. They are not receiving luxuries, they are offered a clean place to live in their dying days; some have shared rooms, there are clothes available from donations, arts/crafts supplies are donated, classes are given by volunteers. This is a remarkable example of public/private/volunteer collaboration to support these least of us in their times of need. If anyone would like me to speak directly to the time my sister spent at The Inn Between, I am sheltering at home (I live in the Liberty Wells section of SLCity) during this time of Coved19. My telephone number is ███████. this is my email and I can use ZOOM. I can't imagine the impact of Coved 19 on the poor and homeless population of SLCity and that The Inn Between may be the last option for more people next year than this year. This is not the time to cut their funds. Please reconsider. Very truly, Linda Griffen

We simply cannot turn our back on such a vulnerable population. At the least, we should fund at previous levels if not beyond, given the difficult time that we're in. Logic would lead one to anticipate the population served by The INN Between is going to be more vulnerable to COVID19 and thus in need of their services. And, God forbid, should the infection result in more people dying before they need to be admitted to The INN Between, there will still be people who will be in need of hospice care for other reasons. This facility is desperately needed by the community much less by those whom it serves. The dignity conveyed upon the dying is shared by those who exhibit such compassion. The city funds a small but critical amount of the facility's needs, but it's probably that many corporate and personal contributions will be less this year than in the past. Thank you for your consideration of this. I could argue that this facility is needed even more than Allen Park. Please prove to me that my community cares more for people than for birds. (I love birds and agree that we deserve to have them in our midst, but not at the expense of caring for a human being as they die). Susan Wieck
